# Golden Rules for Agentic Engineering

Author: Indrajeet Patil
Format: Quarto RevealJS presentation
Canonical URL: https://www.indrapatil.com/agentic-engineering-golden-rules/
Source: https://github.com/IndrajeetPatil/agentic-engineering-golden-rules/
License: CC0 1.0 Universal
Publication date: 2026-10-08
Language: English

## Summary

This slide deck presents nine golden rules for agentic engineering: using coding agents to boost productivity without compromising quality. Quality depends on the engineering system around the agent: a codebase that is easy to navigate, a deterministic harness that gives fast feedback, observable acceptance criteria, prepared codebase patterns, clean context, useful tools, repeatable automation, end-to-end flow improvements, and a team culture that keeps humans responsible for what ships.

The talk is aimed at software engineers who ship production software and have at least some experience with coding agents such as Claude Code or GitHub Copilot CLI.

## The agentic stack

A single tabbed slide introduces the same responsibility diagram for Anthropic, OpenAI, and GitHub Copilot. An LLM reasons and requests tools; the harness manages context, session state, permissions, and tool execution. The agent is the model and harness working in a task loop. Tool-calling sends an action request and returns its result. A desktop app is the user interface, and model access is a separate service. Examples: Claude Desktop Code tab / Claude Code harness / Claude / Anthropic; ChatGPT desktop Codex workspace / Codex harness / GPT / OpenAI; VS Code Copilot interface / Copilot harness / selected Claude model / Anthropic as model developer, with access through GitHub Copilot. Selecting Claude within Copilot does not select the Claude Code harness. The diagrams show responsibilities, not deployment boundaries.

## The golden rules
1. Prepare the codebase for agents. Agents tend to reproduce patterns the repository exposes, including uneven or suboptimal ones. Pay down high-impact technical debt, make sound conventions easy to find, and establish reliable checks before scaling agent work; this helps prevent existing problems from being repeated in new changes.
2. Improve developer experience. If humans hunt for context, agents burn tokens too. Clear structure, one-command workflows (such as make setup and make qa), deterministic QA, living documentation (including a short AGENTS.md), and modular design help humans and agents alike.
3. Set deterministic quality gates. Fast feedback beats orchestration. Use a deterministic harness (formatters, linters, type checkers, behaviour-focused tests, Git hooks, secret, dependency, and infrastructure scans, and accessibility audits) to keep the agent's non-determinism in check. A Ruff F841 example shows how the agent can fix a reported issue, rerun the check, and hand a passing change to human review. Invest in one reliable command that checks the agreed gates and run the same gates in CI; human review still checks whether the work solves the right problem. Never weaken a check merely to get green; repairing an inappropriate gate is deliberate, reviewed work.
4. Define done before delegating. Combine intent with observable acceptance criteria: state the outcome, constraints, what must stay unchanged, and the evidence needed to accept the result. Prescribe steps when sequence matters, such as migrations, incident response, or proven diagnostics. Reproduce bugs before fixing them, inspect rendered UI interactions, and measure performance under comparable conditions. Implementation and tests can share a misunderstanding; compare both with the requirements. Agents verify their own work, inspect results, fix failures, and re-check before handing over evidence for human review.
5. Maintain session hygiene. Coherent context beats haunted context. Long sessions accumulate stale assumptions and conflicting instructions. Default to one task per session, but keep a closely related follow-up in the same session when its reasoning and discoveries still help; restarting can lose a constraint or a failed hypothesis. Length matters as well as coherence, because recall degrades as context grows (context rot); clear context between unrelated tasks and compact only when continuing related work. Use one Git worktree per parallel task so each task has its own working directory, and keep durable conventions, decisions, and lessons in the repository (for example, AGENTS.md) rather than in chat history. Reset with a compact handoff: goal, constraints, relevant files, approaches already ruled out, and acceptance checks.
6. Know thy tools. Sometimes the unlock is a hidden tool affordance. Example affordances that users miss include Claude Code voice dictation, Codex built-in image generation, and GitHub Copilot CLI computer use. Read the changelog; these examples are not exhaustive. Official docs were checked on 8 October 2026. When results are poor, check whether the agent had the right context, tools, and feedback.
7. Automate repeated agent work. Capture effective recurring workflows in prompts, skills, slash commands, and multi-step workflows. Choose the smallest reusable mechanism that fits the work; automate coordination and retain human evaluation of evidence, trade-offs, and decisions about what ships.
8. Identify and remove bottlenecks. Apply Amdahl’s law as an analogy across the SDLC: accelerating implementation alone cannot remove time spent waiting for review, verification, or release. Locate the current queue, choose a targeted intervention, and measure the full flow again because the constraint can move. Examples include deterministic quality gates for inconsistent quality enforcement, an LLM reviewer loop for large PRs, and task-specific end-to-end tests for slow behaviour checks. The reviewer loop adds capacity; it does not replace human judgement.
9. Be curious. Be humble. Be kind. DHH’s “It’s more fun to be competent” line encourages engineers to keep understanding their systems and building their skills as tools change.
